Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

mutter verb

also mumble, murmur, say under one’s breath

classical

Liv. 33.31: clam mussantēs (Lewis & Short; not in Cicero or Caesar)
Traupman 349

mussō, mussāre, mussāvī, mussātum

verb, first conjugation

mutter, murmur, speak under one’s breath

Varro derives it from the sound mū, the least a mute man can say (L.L. 7.101): rightly, an imitative word. Lewis & Short notes that it is not used by Cicero or Caesar.

Other words

  • murmurō, murmurāre — murmur, grumble

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Mil. 3.1.149: servī murmurant, of grumbling (Lewis & Short)

  • muttiō (mūtiō), muttīre, muttīvī — mutter, make a sound: mostly of the peep one is forbidden to make

    verb, fourth conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 381: Etiam muttīs? — Jam tacēbō.; Ter. And. 505: nihil jam muttīre audeō

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

    From the sound mū. Etiam muttīs? is “Still muttering?”, that is, “Not another word!”

  • mussitō, mussitāre — keep quiet, say nothing aloud; mutter under one’s breath

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Mil. 477: mussitābis: plūs oportet scīre servom quam loquī; Liv. 1.50 (Lewis & Short)

    The frequentative of mussō; not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Nimis crūdum est hoc pōmum. — Quid tū mussās?

    This apple is too green. — What are you muttering?Vīv. Exerc. 24

  • Etiam muttīs? — Jam tacēbō.

    Still muttering? — I’ll be quiet now.Plaut. Amph. 381–381b

  • Ergō, sī sapis, mussitābis: plūs oportet scīre servom quam loquī.

    So, if you’re wise, you’ll keep your mouth shut: a slave ought to know more than he says.Plaut. Mil. 476b–477

SourcesLewis & Short: musso · Lewis & Short: murmuro · Lewis & Short: mutio · Lewis & Short: mussito
